summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ , a man with secondary progressive multiple sclerosis and a history of cervical spine surgery, was admitted due to worsening leg weakness that impaired his ability to transfer from his wheelchair. He had no fever or systemic signs of infection, but urinalysis and initial culture indicated a urinary tract infection with E. coli and Enterococcus, likely triggered by his chronic catheterization. He was treated with IV ampicillin-sulbactam for five days, with repeat cultures showing no growth, indicating resolution of infection. His weakness was attributed to an MS pseudo-flare secondary to the UTI. He was evaluated by physical therapy and deemed to require inpatient rehabilitation. Medications were adjusted at discharge to optimize spasticity management, including dose changes to baclofen and tizanidine. He was also noted to have a stage I pressure ulcer on his hip, managed with preventive measures. He was discharged to an extended care facility for rehabilitation with follow-up planned with his MS and urology specialists.
